steps: Plan location & framing
Plan fireplace, chimney and options together; pick a spot that avoids cutting joists. Keep combustibles no closer than the standoffs and leave clearance spaces empty.

• Check restrictions and permits with the local authority having jurisdiction.
  • No special floor reinforcement is needed.
  • No recessed shelves or cupboards in the enclosure above the fireplace; it must stay air space.
  • Run the chimney inside the house if possible; outside, enclose it in an insulated chase. A cold chimney causes poor draft.
  • Finish the enclosure's interior walls flat.
  • If options that need power may be added later, run the wiring during framing.

Framing dimensions appear only on the Figure 4 diagram (p. 8); the manual notes they are larger than required.
Anchor it & fit the top standoff
Screw the legs to the floor through the pre-cut holes. Screw on the top standoff, bend its back shield to 45° and keep at least a ¼" air gap to the 2x4 framing.

The top standoff, with its built-in heat shield, must be installed. Do not fill the gap between the fireplace and the standoff; the finishing material covers it. Nothing, combustible or not, may be placed below the header supports of the top standoff.
Outside air duct (if used)
Open the outside air cover under the unit, fit the rotating elbow and run insulated flex duct to a wall inlet; seal the joints with aluminum tape.

1. Remove the outside air cover on the bottom of the fireplace (four screws) and break out its central part.
  2. Attach the 4" aluminium duct to the elbow inlet with metal screws and aluminum tape.
  3. Pull any plastic cover back so none is under the fireplace or within 3" of it; tape the insulation.
  4. Fit the elbow and support with at least two of the removed screws, aim it, tighten and tape the joint.
  5. Cut a 4 ¼" hole (5 ¼" for 5" duct) in the outside wall, push the inlet in from outside and seal it.
  6. Screw the duct to the inlet sleeve, then re-cover it with insulation and tape.
Don't crimp the duct at corners; it restricts the combustion airflow.
Facing & faceplate
Remove the faceplate (5/32 Allen key) and bottom louver first. Facing must be non-combustible; gypsum or other combustibles may not touch the casing.

• Never cover the decorative faceplate or its louvers.
  • There is only 1" between the faceplate and the fireplace body: enough for ½" cement board, ⅛" adhesive and ⅜" tile. Thicker finishes such as brick or stone stop at the faceplate, which can serve as a template.
  • Drywall stops at the side and top standoffs; the front face of the top standoff counts as fireplace facing.
  • The minimum non-combustible facing size is shown only as a diagram (Figure 9, p. 12).
  • The manual recommends removing the door until all finishing work is done.
Chimney
6" ICC Model EXCEL only. Frame 12" square openings, fit a radiation shield at each floor (shield and storm collar in the attic) and fix the first length with the three screws provided.

1. Keep 2" or more to combustibles, with no insulation in that space.
  2. Extend at least 3' above the roof contact and 2' above any wall, roof or building within 10'; use a roof brace if more than 5' above the roof.
  3. Fit the roof radiation shield (XM-6ERRS) so it extends 3" above the roof line.
  4. Flashing: vented if the chimney is enclosed to the roof, regular if not. Don't block the vented flashing's openings.
  5. Seal the storm collar with exterior sealant below and on top (not roofing tar), then secure the rain cap.

Follow the EXCEL chimney installation manual for supports, bracing and anchors.
Offsets (if needed)
Max. 30° in the USA (45° in Canada) and four elbows. Three metal screws per joint; a roof, wall or offset support above each offset.

An elbow may go directly on top of the fireplace. Elbows don't support the chimney above an offset. Through a combustible exterior wall, use an angled wall insulated radiation shield (XM-6EWRSI30 or XM-6EWRSI45), and leave off its outside plate if the chimney is enclosed outside. A non-combustible wall needs no shield: fill gaps with rock wool and seal with silicone.
Masonry chimney (if used)
Run EXCEL chimney from the fireplace to a listed stainless-steel liner fitted inside the clay liner, joined with the masonry adaptor.

• Liner: EXCEL or listed to ULC-S635, ULC-S640 or UL-1777, all the way to the top of the masonry chimney.
  • Adaptor: 3 stainless steel rivets to the liner, 3 screws to the EXCEL chimney.
  • At least one 18" EXCEL length after the elbow; where it enters the masonry, 12" min. from the ceiling.
  • An existing chimney must first be inspected by an authority having jurisdiction and serve this fireplace only. Under 8"x8" inside, a listed flexible liner with the LM-6LAF adaptor can be used.
Note: The text on p. 17 gives the masonry adaptor's part number as FO-FDM6, while the Figure 16 label on the same page lists FO-FDM7 and FO-FDM6.
Hearth extension & spark guard
Non-combustible hearth at least 18" deep and 36½" wide, centered. On a combustible floor, the provided 5" x 36" spark guard goes half under the unit, half under the hearth.

The guard is centered on the door opening and extends 2½" beneath the fireplace. It isn't needed on a non-combustible floor. Raised units need a site-built guard, at least 36" wide and centered on the door opening:

  • Z-shaped if the base of the unit is 2 ½" or less above the hearth flooring; its height equals that gap and it goes at least 2½" under both the hearth and the fireplace.
  • Right-angle if higher; sides at least 2½" x 2½", covered with non-combustible material.
Refractory bricks & ash lip

Before the first fire: rear brick, right and left sides, soft insulation on the firebox floor, the bottom brick, then the two front bricks. Seat the ash lip's rear edge behind the firebox's vertical lip.
The bricks are made for this model and need no modification. To remove them, reverse the sequence. Figure 20 identifies the left and right pieces.

panels.title: Smoke when the door opens
items: Door opened too quickly → open it slowly and let the pressure stabilize
Dirty chimney or plugged cap; screened caps clog with creosote
Chimney too short for the altitude and number of elbows (Table 4)
Inline blower, range hood or bath fan running → negative pressure; crack a nearby window
Too little kindling; smoke is most likely during lighting

panels.title: Burns too fast or won't slow down
items: Air leaking past door seals or gaskets → paper test, replace seals
Hard to slow the burn or shorter burn times → worn door gasket (FO-GRK9)
Air control has no effect → air leak, likely at the door; stop using it until fixed
Unwanted hole in a secondary air tube at the top of the firebox
Connector behind the top louver glows red → over-firing

panels.title: Smolders or hard to light
items: Too little combustion air → reopen the control, wait longer before restricting
Wet or unseasoned wood → excess visible smoke, poor burn, dark glass
Weak draft → smoke in the room, hard to light; adding chimney height is the usual fix
Weak draft is often mistaken for a blocked air intake

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
Before you start, move the combustion air lever all the way open (to the right). You want as much air as possible while lighting.

Top-down fire (the method the manual recommends)

  1. Build the fire behind the front bricks. Lay 2-3 criss-crossed layers of small wood, about 10 pieces 1" to 2" in diameter.
  2. Criss-cross about 20 finger-sized pieces of kindling on top, then add a few pieces of paper.
  3. Light the top of the pile. Close the door most of the way, but not completely. You should see air rushing in.
  4. After about 2 minutes, close the door completely. If the fire starts to smolder, crack the door for another minute or two, then close it.
  5. Once the startup wood is a bed of coals, rake the coals to the front and add up to 6 logs: bottom layer front to back, next layer left to right.
  6. Keep the door cracked for a couple of minutes while the logs catch, then close it. Leave the air lever on maximum until your next reload.

Prefer the traditional way? Crumple paper under 3 or 4 criss-crossed layers of kindling, light the paper, and keep the door about 1" from closed at first.

A taller chimney or a colder day means the door needs to stay cracked a little longer at startup.
Never use flammable liquids or a grate. Never leave the fire burning with the door open or ajar, and keep the fire behind the front step.

air.title: The two air controls
air.html:
Your fireplace has two separate air controls.

Combustion air lever: how fast it burns

There's no chimney damper. The closed door seals the fire, and this lever sets how much air gets in. Move it right to open (more air) and left to close.

  • Close it gradually, never from maximum to minimum at once.
  • If the fire dies down and smolders, open it again and wait longer before turning it down.
  • Always keep a visible flame; it keeps the glass and chimney clean. In some homes the lever can't be fully closed without losing the fire, and that's normal.

Outside air control: where the air comes from

It's behind the bottom louver; pull the louver off to reach it. Lever facing forward: open to outside air. Lever pointing up: closed, so the fire uses room air. If your fireplace is connected to outside air, keep it open while you burn. Close it when the fireplace isn't burning, or if it isn't connected, to keep cold air out.

Lever has no effect on the fire? Air is leaking in, most likely at the door gasket. Stop using the fireplace until the leak is fixed. The replacement gasket kit is FO-GRK9.

reload.title: Reloading the fire
reload.html:
1. Have the next load of wood ready before you open the door. The firebox cools while the door is open.
  2. Turn off the blower if you have one. A running fan can make smoke spill into the room.
  3. Open the door slowly so smoke doesn't spill out.
  4. Poke and stir the leftover wood to revive the fire, then add the new logs.
  5. Keep a clear path in front of the metal tube centered at the front of the firebox (the manual calls it the pilot). It brings air to the coals.
  6. Leave the door slightly open for a couple of minutes until the new wood is well lit, then close it and set the air lever where you want it.
Smoke coming into the room? Check that kitchen and bathroom exhaust fans are off. They create negative pressure that pulls smoke out of the fireplace.

If you have the optional blower, wait about 20 minutes after reloading before turning it back on.

Heat vs. burn time: more air gives more heat but burns through wood faster and costs efficiency. If the fire burns too quickly, turn the air down. If it smolders with no visible flames, turn the air up.

wood.title: What wood to burn
wood.html:
Burn seasoned cordwood: wood that has been cut, split and left to dry under cover for at least 6 months, preferably a year or more. Dry seasoned wood is generally under 20% moisture, and the manual strongly suggests a wood moisture meter to check.

  • Wet wood is hard to burn, gives little heat, builds up creosote and leaves dark deposits on the glass.
  • Hardwoods burn longer and more evenly, because you can fit more weight of wood in the firebox.
  • Densified fuel logs are fine on their own or mixed with wood.

Never burn

Driftwood, treated wood, coal, garbage, plastic or scrap. Large amounts of paper, cardboard, mill ends or construction waste can over-fire and damage the fireplace. Don't use construction scraps such as 2x4 or plywood as your only fuel.

Wax firelogs (such as Duraflame) aren't recommended because they dirty the glass. If you use one, burn only one at a time, don't poke or stir it, and use only firelogs evaluated for fireplace use.

firstfires.title: Your first few fires
firstfires.html:
Expect a slow start during the first few fires. That's normal.

Black bricks

The refractory bricks lining the firebox hold moisture from manufacturing. It takes a few hot fires to dry them out. Until then they look black with smoke deposits. Once the moisture is gone, they turn white.

No break-in needed

Unlike a cast iron stove, this fireplace doesn't need curing with small fires that slowly get bigger. You can build a large fire from the very start.

A slight smell

Curing paint and oil burning off the metal cause an odor during the first few fires. It can be strong enough to set off your smoke detector. Open doors and windows to air out the room.

Before the very first fire, the refractory bricks must be properly installed inside the firebox.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
In a controlled-combustion firebox, the fire isn't always hot enough to keep the glass clean. A good hot fire once a day usually burns off most deposits. The drier the wood and the hotter the fire, the cleaner the glass.

Cleaning it

  1. Wait until the glass is cool. Cleaning hot glass can cause a serious burn.
  2. For light buildup, dampen a ball of newspaper and dip it in the fireplace ashes to make a paste. Scrub the glass with it and wipe clean.
  3. For heavier buildup, use a woodstove glass cleaner recommended by your dealer.
Never use an abrasive cleaner unless it's made for this use. Don't spray glass cleaner on the painted surfaces; it can strip the paint.

Heat won't break the glass, but an impact can. It's 5mm thick ceramic, so be careful not to hit it, and don't slam the door.

ash.title: Emptying the ashes
ash.html:
Take the ashes out before they get too deep, that is, before they start spilling when you open the door.

  1. Put the ashes in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid.
  2. Set the closed container on a non-combustible floor or on the ground, well away from anything that can burn.
  3. If you'll bury or spread the ashes, keep them in the closed container until all the cinders have thoroughly cooled.

The ash lip

A removable ash lip keeps ashes from piling up at the front of the fireplace. To take it out or put it back, hold it at an angle and lower it into place. Make sure its rear edge sits behind the vertical lip of the firebox.

chimney.title: Chimney & creosote
chimney.html:
A slow fire gives off tar and vapors that condense in the chimney as creosote. If creosote catches fire, it burns extremely hot.

  • Check the chimney for creosote every week or so until experience shows how often it needs cleaning.
  • Clean it once buildup reaches 1/8" (3 mm) or more.
  • Soot or creosote more than 1/8" (3 mm) thick means the chimney needs immediate cleaning. You should also check it more often, and you may need to change how you burn.

How it's swept

  1. Remove the front burn tube. Then slide the baffle, the hard insulation panel above the tubes, toward the front and out through the door opening.
  2. Close the fireplace door.
  3. Remove the chimney cap and sweep with a 6" round soft bristle brush.
  4. Put the baffle and tube back the same way, tube holes facing slightly upward, and insert the locking pin.
Dry wood and a visible flame help keep the chimney clean. Wet wood increases creosote buildup.

safety.title: Safety & over-firing
safety.html:
• Keep furniture, firewood and other combustibles at least 4' from the front of the fireplace.
  • Burn with the door fully closed. A partly open door can draw gas and flame out of the fireplace.
  • Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen a fire.
  • Have at least one smoke detector on each level of your home and at least one carbon monoxide detector.
  • Don't use a grate, don't tamper with the air control, and don't install an insert, a gas log set or a gas log lighter in this fireplace.
  • Do not over-fire the fireplace.

Signs of over-firing

You're over-firing if you can't slow the fire down, or if the chimney connector behind the top louver glows red. Damage from over-firing isn't covered by the warranty.

Burning fast and out of control? Check the door seals and gaskets for air leaks, and have the secondary air tubes at the top of the firebox inspected for holes.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
RSF warrants its wood-burning fireplaces against defects in material and workmanship for 30 years. What's covered changes over time:

First yearDefective parts repaired or replaced, plus reasonable labor
Years 2 through 5Defective parts repaired or replaced; no labor
Years 6 through 30Replacement parts, if available, at 50% of the published retail price; no labor

Not covered

  • Glass. Electrical components are covered for one year only.
  • Normal wear: paint discoloration, worn gaskets, eroded or cracked refractory or baffle.
  • Vandalism, neglect, abuse, over-firing, improper fuel or fuel loads, or skipped service.
  • Installations that don't follow the manual, damage in transit, and repairs RSF didn't authorize in advance.
The warranty isn't transferable, and non-genuine parts void it. This is a summary; the official PDF has the full terms.

specChimney.html:
Certified chimney6" ICC Model EXCEL only
Min. height, fireplace top to below rain cap12' standard · 8' mobile home
Max. height, fireplace top to below rain cap36' (13,72 m)
Max. height supported by the fireplace20'
Clearance to combustibles2" or more, no insulation
Framing rough opening12" square, never smaller
Above the roof3' above roof contact · 2' above anything within 10'
Offsetsmax. 30° USA · 45° Canada · four elbows max.

Raise the minimum height about 6" for every 1000' of elevation; each offset (pair of elbows) adds more. Table 4 gives the recommended minimums: at 6015', for example, 15' for a straight chimney and 18'6" with one 30° offset. Use a roof brace if the chimney is more than 5' above the roof. Do not install a flue damper.

Note: Table 1 on p. 6 prints the maximum chimney height as 36' with (13,72 m) beside it, and those two values are not the same length.

specClear.html:

Nothing, combustible or not, may sit below the header supports of the top standoff. Overall unit dimensions and the clearance drawing are shown only as figures (Figures 1 and 2, pp. 5-6).

specMantel.title: Combustible mantel & posts
specMantel.html:

Non-combustible mantels can go anywhere around the facing; if one sits below the combustible-mantel height, cover the wall between the facing and the mantel with non-combustible material. A shelf with a variable cross-section must keep both its widest part and its lowest point at or above the height for their depth.

specHearth.title: Hearth extension
specHearth.html:
Min. depth, from the front of the fireplace18" (457 mm)
Min. total width, centered on the firebox opening36½" (927 mm)
Min. spark guard width36" (914 mm)

Protect the area in front of the fireplace with a non-combustible material such as brick, tile, stone or slate. No minimum thickness is required. On a combustible floor, the provided 5" x 36" sheet-metal spark guard goes under the joint between fireplace and hearth; raised installations need a site-built Z-shaped or right-angle guard (see the install sequence).

specAir.title: Outside air
specAir.html:
Ductinsulated aluminium flex, rated over 200° F
Diameter4" if the total run is under 25'; 5" for longer runs
Max. vertical rise above the unit base12'
Inletat least 5' below the chimney rain cap; never in an attic
Wall hole4 ¼" (5 ¼" for 5" duct)
Suggested kitFO-INT (4")

Not required unless local code calls for it or the fireplace is in a mobile home. The rotating elbow at the base can exit in any direction. A 5" run starts in 4" to clear the base, then steps up through a 4"-5" increaser. Keep any plastic duct cover at least 3" from the fireplace, and include a P-trap loop in the duct to avoid condensation.

specMobile.title: Mobile home requirements
specMobile.html:
Bedroom or sleeping roomnot permitted
Outside air kitrequired (FO-INT recommended)
Chimney capERCS spark screen required
Floor anchoringtwo #8 wood screws, at least 1 ½" long, through the bottom standoffs
Min. ceiling clearance7'
Min. chimney height8'

Applies to manufactured homes, mobile homes and transportable buildings. If the chimney exits through the wall 7 feet (2.1m) or less above ground level, enclose it in a chase. A radiation shield is required at the ceiling/roof, running completely through the cavity to the outermost plane of the roof (it may be trimmed flush). Keep the floor, walls and ceiling/roof structurally intact.

In some circumstances, the 8' minimum chimney gives dirtier glass than 12' of chimney.

review.notes: One combined owner's manual (installation + operation). Shown only as figures, not transcribed: unit dimensions (Fig. 1, p. 5), clearance drawing (Fig. 2, p. 6), framing examples (Fig. 4, p. 8), minimum non-combustible facing (Fig. 9, p. 12); the Complete Options List (pp. 29-30) has no extractable text, and Replacement Parts (p. 31) says only 'Will be available soon.' Fig. 25 (p. 26) carries a 5/16" label with no explaining text; not used. Catalog height/width/depth, weight, firebox volume, max log length, glass/view area and heating area are not in the manual text, so they were not checked. The side standoff to firebox opening distance is printed '81/8”' (p. 5) and is given as 8 1/8". The manual calls the unit a 'fireplace Insert' (p. 4) and 'your Insert' (p. 24), and the ash lip section (p. 21) says 'Focus 3600B'; treated as copy errors. The provided spark guard is 5" x 36" while the Table 1 (I) minimum width is 36", yet p. 19 says it can be cut to that minimum; left as printed. The metal air tube at the front of the firebox is called 'the pilot' (p. 24); owner text explains it. Troubleshooting mentions an 'inline blower' (p. 25); the options list the Internal Blower FO-FDHB9 (p. 4). No code table, so codes are empty. No French-only or scrambled text.
